L908@P41: Again concerning the case of Hirzebruch, it is not clear to me whether
L909@P41: the idea of his coming to Princeton next year came from him or from Princeton.
L910@P41: May I ask which is the case ? My personal view is that, when a mathematician
L911@P41: such as Hirzebruch expresses a definite wish to spend a year in such and such
L912@P41: a place, one ought to try to accommodate him as far as possible; on the other
L913@P41: hand, if the whole thing merely means that he could be persuaded to come to
L914@P41: Princeton if sufficient pressure is exerted on him, the arguments in favor
L915@P41: of his coming would be much less strong. Perhaps you have already heard that
L916@P41: Grothendieck has a purely algebraic theory covering all of Hirzebruch's results
L917@P41: on the Riemann-Roch theorem (at the moment, Grothendieck still has to assume
L918@P41: characteristic O). Thus it might be more , important for Hirzebruch to learn
L919@P41: about this than to re-visit a place like Princeton, where after all, he already
L920@P41: knows everybody and may not have such a great deal to learn. Such points
L921@P41: certainly should be taken into consideration when arranging for our invitations.
L922@P41: In this connection, it occurs to me that Grothendieck has never, I believe,
L923@P41: been invited to the Institute. ''ihY is that so?
L924@P41: Concerning L. J. Brouwer, I was told in Holland that for a number of years
L925@P41: there has been virtually no contact between him and any .tutch mathematician,
L926@P41: or even logician, and that he lives in almost complete retirement. In view
L927@P41: of this, and of his present age, I cannot imagine what would be the point of
L928@P41: inviting him to Princeton, except as an interesting relic of former and perhaps
L929@P41: more exciting times.
L930@P41: I am tentatively planning to come to Princeton for a few weeks in January
L931@P41: and February (roughly speaking, from January 15 to February lS), and try to
L932@P41: solve my housing problem. .Jould it be possible to reserve a small apartment
L933@P41: for me in the Project, for that period? My family would of course remain in
L934@P41: Paris.
L935@P41: vJith best wishes, I am
L936@P41: Very truly yours,
L937@P41: /s/ A. vv eil

L653@P30: During the last decade the theory of linear partial differential
L654@P30: equations has undergone a rapid expansion making it one of today9 s most active
L655@P30: fields of mathematics. It has been cultivated particularly by American, French,
L656@P30: Russian and Scandinavian mathematicians. Some of the names prominently connected with this development arej in this country: Calderon, Friedrichs~
L657@P30: John, Lewy and Nirenberg; in France g Leray I Lions, Malgrange and Schwartz;
L658@P30: in Russia: Ladyzenskaja, Petrowsky, Sobolev and Visik; in Scandinavia:
L659@P30: G~rding and HBrmander .
L660@P30: The youngest in this group is Lars H8rmander, born in Sweden in 1931
L661@P30: and professor at the University of Stockholm since 1957. He received his basic
L662@P30: scientific education at Lund University with supplementary studies pursued at
L663@P30: Sorbonne and other European mathematical centers. He visited the University of
L664@P30: Chicago and New York University in 1956 and was a member of the Institute for
L665@P30: Advanced Study in 1960=1961.
L666@P30: H8rrnander 1 s thesis, his first major work on differential operators,
L667@P30: appeared in 1955 in Acta Mathematica. It was exceptionally rich in new ideas
L668@P30: and results. Instead of adhering to the traditional trend of studying only
L669@P30: special types of equations, H8rmander set forth a new and broader goal: to
L670@P30: develop a general theory for linear differential operators. At least some of
L671@P30: his results· ought to be mentioned here in spite of their technical nature. One
L672@P30: of the fundamental problems was to determine the relative strength of two
L673@P30: operators and to trace this and similar concepts back to their algebraic origin
L674@P30: hidden within the operator polynomials. This project was brilliantly carried
L675@P30: through in Chapter II for the case of constant coefficients. The results were
L676@P30: partly extended to the case of variable coefficientB later in the paper. The
L677@P30: analytic core of his method consisted of a systematically developed algebra of
L678@P30-31: quadratic integrals. With this technique H8rmander obtained a far=reaching - 2 -
L679@P31: extension of the energy integral method$ previously used in special cases by
L680@P31: Lewyj Friedrichs and Leray. Guided by this method H6rmander introduced the
L681@P31: notion of operators of principal type 1 a concept which in a further developed
L682@P31: form became of great importance in his researcho His results included the
L683@P31: first and only existence theorem valid for a general class of non-elliptic
L684@P31: operators with smooth but not analytic coefficientso
L685@P31: H6rmander's thesis gave rise to a rich literature, with himself as a
L686@P31: frequent contributor. In a series of subsequent papers he gave valuable
L687@P31: contributions to a great variety of problems on differential operators including
L688@P31: existence and properties of fundamental solutions, uniqueness of the Cauchy
L689@P31: problem j inner regularity and boundary regularity of solutions, to name a few o
L690@P31: This part of his production is characterized by the same skill and power previously shown in the thesis. Two of these papers contain outstanding accompLlshments to which we shall return later.
L691@P31: Outside his main field of interestj H6rmander has to his credit significant achievements particularly in harmonic analysis and the theory of distributionso In 1958 the Polish mathematician tojasiewicz and H8rmander shared the
L692@P31: credit of solving a difficult problem raised by L. Schwartz concerning the
L693@P31: divieibility of a distribution by a polynomial of several variables. H8rmander
L694@P31: base:i a skillfully organized proof on Whitneyvs extension theorem combined with
L695@P31: an algebraic lemma by Seidenberg and Tarski~ earlier used in the thesis. - A
L696@P31: major paper is devoted to translation invariant operators in Lebesgue spaces
L697@P31: and to the real variable method introduced by Calderon and Zygmund o His approach
L698@P31: admitted a unified treatment of the problems in this field and it gave simplified
L699@P31: proofs and significant extensions of previous results. The paper is of great
L700@P31: '< value although some of the results still leave room for further studies.
L701@P31: In 1957 Hans Lewy constructed an example showing that a linear
L702@P31: inhomogeneous equ~tion with highly regular coefficients nevertheless might fail
L703@P31-32: ... I
L704@P32: = 3 -
L705@P32: to have a solution in any open set. This disturbing fact spurred H8rmander to
L706@P32: a renewed investigation of operators with variable coefficients. He extended
L707@P32: the concept of operators of principal type and discovered, after a penetrating
L708@P32: analysis, that one term in the so-called commutator was the deciding factor for
L709@P32: the existence of solutions. His deep-going study resulted in a new and more
L710@P32: sophisticated kind of existence theoremsj answering the questions brought to
L711@P32: light by Lewy's example. For this achievement Harmander received in 1962 the
L712@P32: Fields Medal, the most distinguished international award in mathematics.
L713@P32: H8rmander is also the author of the first major monograph on the
L714@P32: modern theory of partial differential equations. The book is announced to
L715@P32: appear during February 1963.
L716@P32: Harmander 1 s flawless production bears testimony to a well-organized
L717@P32: scientific mind of great creativeness and power. His work has made him one
L718@P32: of the leading younger mathematicians in the world today. In his main field
L719@P32: he is unquestionably the leading figure .
